chapter_metadata.title: Endobronchial Silicone Stents for Airway Management
chapter_metadata.reference: Principles and Practice of Interventional Pulmonology, 2025

definitions.definition: Trachea, main stem bronchi and—in select cases—lobar bronchi.
Postintubation or posttracheostomy tracheal stenoses (simple vs complex).

technology_and_technique.summary: Gold‑standard silicone stent; straight, hourglass, and bifurcated/Y designs; external studs reduce migration; radiopaque (barium sulfate/gold) and new transparent variant; requires rigid bronchoscopy; easily repositioned/removed; on‑site customization feasible.

Polyethylene threads embedded in silicone; thinner walls (better inner/outer diameter ratio); sharper edges; slightly smoother outer surface → higher migration vs Dumon; visible via tungsten spots; deployed from a semirigid tube; operator skill similar to Dumon.
Hood (silicone) and Noppen (Tygon) straight stents exist but are less commonly advertised/used; newer self‑expanding metal stents have replaced some indications.
Radiopaque markers facilitate positioning and follow‑up; transparent Dumon allows mucosal visualization behind the wall while preserving radio‑opacity.

recommendations: Consider silicone airway stent for airway luminal diameter reduction >50%.
Counteract extrinsic compression from tumors or lymph nodes.
Stabilize airway after endoscopic removal of intraluminal tumor.
Treat benign strictures (selected).
Stabilize collapsing airways (malacia, polychondritis) with caution.
Seal airway fistulas (stump dehiscences, tracheo/broncho‑esophageal).
Purely intrinsic: debulk; consider stent as bridge to chemoradiotherapy, for high local‑recurrence risk, or after oncologic therapy failure.
Mixed intrinsic/extrinsic: multimodality debulking + stent insertion.
Extrinsic only: dilatation followed by stenting.
Avoid upfront stenting in treatment‑naïve patients if oncologic therapy can promptly relieve obstruction.
Life‑threatening obstruction: few absolute contraindications; use other techniques first when feasible (e.g., laser debulking).
Benign disease: prefer removable stents until multidisciplinary team confirms inoperability.
Airway instability (malacia): seldom a good indication for permanent stenting.
Use rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia for silicone stent deployment.
Perform mechanical debulking and dilation prior to insertion as needed.
Stent length should extend 5 mm above and below the abnormality.
Diameter guidance: trachea 14–16 mm; mainstem bronchi 12–13 mm; bronchus intermedius 10–11 mm.
For fistulas and tracheobronchomalacia, oversize slightly (no anchoring lesion).
Avoid distal pushing during placement due to perforation risk.
If incomplete opening, use balloon or rigid instruments to complete expansion.
Reassess and replace stents annually until no longer indicated.
Migration → extract under rigid bronchoscopy; replace with appropriate size; consider percutaneous external fixation in select cases.
Granulation at stent margins → mechanical or thermal therapy (laser, cautery, cryotherapy); replace stent if required.
Mucoid impaction → reduce risk via humidification with sterile normal saline nebulization 2–3 times daily; remove/replace if obstructed.
Prefer silicone for most indications including benign disease; avoid metal stents in benign disease (fully silicone‑covered metal may be an exception).
To preserve ventilation to covered lobes (e.g., RUL with Y stents), consider fenestrations or distal limb add‑on stents (Borgne Y).

clinical_procedures.name: Silicone stent deployment (rigid bronchoscopy)
steps: Induce general anesthesia; perform rigid bronchoscopy.
Pre‑treat: mechanical tumor debulking and/or airway dilation as needed.
Measure lesion length endoscopically; confirm CT‑based estimate; select a stent extending 5 mm beyond lesion proximally and distally.
Select diameter based on maximal dilation caliber (trachea 14–16 mm; mainstem 12–13 mm; BI 10–11 mm).
Load stent into introducer; position just distal to lesion; pull back to final position with rigid forceps.
Avoid distal pushing over a pathologic segment; complete expansion with balloon or rigid instruments if needed.
Post‑deploy inspection; schedule follow‑up and annual reassessment/replacement while indicated.

clinical_procedures.name: Temporary stent trial for suspected malacia
steps: Place temporary stent as internal splinting.
If clinical improvement: refer for external stenting; consider stent removal.
If no improvement: remove stent; recommend physiotherapy and CPAP.
clinical_procedures.notes: Straight Dumon is not recommended for malacic stenoses or flexible dyskinetic tracheas due to migration risk.

decreases: Hourglass stent for short benign tracheal disease

summary: Debulk/dilate first; avoid unnecessary upfront stenting in treatment‑naïve malignancy.
Extend coverage 5 mm beyond lesion; diameter by maximal dilation caliber (14–16 mm trachea; 12–13 mm mainstem; 10–11 mm BI).
Avoid distal pushing; use balloon/rigid tools for full expansion; humidify 2–3×/day.
Manage migration, granulation, and secretion impaction proactively; consider external fixation/upsizing when appropriate.
For malacia, use a temporary stent trial; refer for external stenting if improved; otherwise remove and proceed with non‑stent strategies.

management: Prefer silicone stents for most benign and many malignant indications; metal stents should generally be avoided in benign disease (fully silicone‑covered metal may be an exception).
Use hourglass designs for short benign tracheal disease; Y/bifurcated stents for carinal involvement; fenestrations/Borgne Y to preserve lobar ventilation.

points: Dumon silicone stents remain the reference standard due to removability, safety profile, and versatility.
Outcomes depend on proper indications, meticulous rigid‑bronchoscopic deployment, and proactive complication management.
Despite limitations in malacia and curved anatomies, silicone stents are a cost‑effective, reversible option for central airway obstruction and fistulas.
